Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Housing and Economic Development, my name is Greg Payne and I serve as the Senior Advisor on Housing Policy in the Governor's Office of Policy II111OV2l'[lO11 and the Future. I am here today to offer testimony in support of L.D. 2079, An Act to Amend the Laws Governing
Municipal Reporting on Residential Buildings.
This bill seeks to make small changes to important legislation approved last year requiring
certain communities to provide annual information to MOCA about the housing units they
approved for building, demolition and occupancy during the prior calendar year. L.D. 2079 makes this critical information easier for municipalities to provide by aligning the categories of housing with those already sought by the U.S. Census Bureau, and extending the annual
reporting date from January 31" to March 31" .
Understanding the amount and types of housing being built, demolished and occupied in our state each year will allow local, regional and state stakeholders to make better and more
informed decisions about housing policy. We appreciate the work being undertaken to pull such
information together, and support the changes laid out in this bill which will make that task
easier for our local partners.
Thank you for your consideration of our testimony. I would be happy to answer any questions.

TESTIMONY BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON HOUSING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
IN SUPPORT OF LD 2079
An Act to Amend the Laws Governing Municipal Reporting on Residential Buildings
January 20, 2026
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing
and Economic Development, my name is Hilary Gove. I am one of the two Housing Opportunity Program Coordinators within the Maine Office of Community Affairs (MOCA). I am speaking today in support of LD 2079, An Act to Amend the Laws Governing Municipal Reporting on
Residential Buildings
This bill amends the municipal housing data categories that municipalities with 4,000 or more
residents must report to MOCA, as well as extends the deadline for submission of the municipal
data report from the end of January to the end of March of each reporting year. This legislation
also encourages municipalities with fewer than 4,000 residents to report housing data.
MOCA supports this bill because the amended data categories in the bill align with how
municipalities currently report building permit data to the U.S. Census. The U.S. Census asks municipalities to organize building permit data by unit type including single-family, 2-unit, 3-4
unit, and 5 or more units. Aligning the State's data collection process with how municipalities
already collect and report on housing data makes the data collection process easier for
municipalities.
Also, MOCA supports the extension of the reporting deadline from January to March of each year,
to give municipalities additional time to collect and report on yearly housing data.
Finally, MOCA supports the inclusion of language that encourages municipalities with fewer than
4,000 residents to provide housing data. Receiving data from a greater number of municipalities will help to more accurately track the State's progress towards its housing production goals.
Thank you for your time. I would be happy to answer any questions now or at the work session.

Testimony of the Greater Portland Council of Governments In Support of LD 2079 - An Act to Amend the Laws Governing Municipal Reporting on Residential Buildings Dear Members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee: The Greater Portland Council of Governments (GPCOG) supports LD 2079, the fix bill to LD 1184, and appreciates the Legislature's effort to make targeted, practical adjustments to the municipal housing data reporting requirements. GPCOG is coordinating the statewide housing data collection effort in partnership with the Housing Opportunity Program (HOP), and from an implementation standpoint, this fix bill meaningfully improves clarity, consistency, and feasibility for municipalities. The changes proposed in LD 2079 are closely aligned with the recommendations that emerged from last year's pilot project and with how this year's data collection is being structured. The bill keeps the request focused on essential information (building permits, certificates of occupancy or final approvals, and demolitions), while aligning building categories with those used by the Census - except for separately identifying accessory dwelling units, which is important given their role under LD 2003. Together, these changes will allow the State to better understand housing production without overcomplicating the reporting process or placing unnecessary burden on municipal staff. We also support the bill's adjustment to the reporting deadline. Additional flexibility is important, particularly as municipalities adapt to a new annual reporting requirement. This change will help improve data quality while making compliance more manageable for local staff. Overall, LD 2079 reflects a practical, implementation-focused approach that will result in clearer reporting, more reliable data, and better outcomes for both municipalities and the State. For these reasons, GPCOG supports the bill.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the Housing and Economic
Development Committee, my name is Tanya Emery, and I am providing testimony in support of LD 2079 at the direction of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). Our LPC is composed of municipal officials from acrossMaine, elected by their peers to represent member
communities. MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization that aims to help provide
policy solutions that work for all residents of Maine.

LD 2079 makes important improvements over the residential unit reporting bill passed last year. Local govermnents are one of the state's most important partners in addressing Maine's housing crisis. We
understand the desire for consistent reporting on local progress to create residential units. Scaling back the previously enacted reporting requirements, which were onerous, is not only appropriate but necessary so that local govermnent bodies can focus on creating units rather than sourcing data not always available to them for the purpose of reporting it to the state.

MMA's Legislative Policy Committee appreciates and fully supports the language introduced in LD

2079 and the implicit recognition of the need to right-size this effort in coordination with the many other
imperatives assigned to local govermnents in the continued drive to create housing in Maine. We urge the

committee to support LD 2079. Thank you for your time and attention to this matter, and I am happy to
